s: The nations are to hear the LORD's glory, marvelous works, and salvation declared among them, and the families of nations are told to ascribe glory and strength to him. They are also told that the LORD reigns and that he will judge the peoples with equity.

l: gods of the peoples, Psalms, Chapter 96
s: The gods of the peoples are declared to be idols, in contrast to the LORD who made the heavens. The LORD is said to be feared above all gods.

l: judgment (the LORD's coming judgment), Psalms, Chapter 96
s: The LORD is said to be coming to judge the earth, and the coming is stated twice for emphasis. He will judge the peoples with equity, and the world with righteousness and with his truth, and creation is called to rejoice before him because of it.

Chapter 97 proclaims that the LORD reigns and calls the earth and the islands to rejoice. His throne is founded on righteousness and justice, and he appears with clouds, darkness, fire, and lightning, so that the earth trembles and the mountains melt like wax. The heavens declare his righteousness and all peoples see his glory, while those who serve engraved images and boast in idols are to be shamed and all gods are told to worship him. Zion and the daughters of Judah rejoice at his judgments, and the LORD is declared most high above all the earth and all gods. Those who love the LORD are told to hate evil, and are assured that he preserves and delivers them, sowing light and gladness for the righteous and calling them to give thanks to his holy Name.

The LORD reigns, surrounded by clouds and darkness, with righteousness and justice as the foundation of his throne. Fire goes before him and burns up his adversaries, his lightning lights the world, and the mountains melt at his presence. He is most high above all the earth and exalted far above all gods, and he preserves the souls of his saints and delivers them from the wicked.
The earth is called to rejoice, and it sees the LORD's lightning and trembles. The mountains melt like wax at his presence, and he is declared Lord of the whole earth and most high above it.

l: idol worshippers (those who serve engraved images), Psalms, Chapter 97
s: Those who serve engraved images and boast in their idols are to be shamed. The gods they serve are commanded to worship the LORD, who is exalted far above them.

l: righteous people (the LORD's saints), Psalms, Chapter 97
s: Those who love the LORD are told to hate evil, and the LORD preserves their souls and delivers them from the hand of the wicked. Light is sown for the righteous and gladness for the upright in heart, and they are urged to be glad in the LORD and give thanks to his holy Name.

Psalm 98 calls on the earth to sing a new song to the LORD for the marvelous things he has done. His right hand and holy arm have worked salvation, which he has made known and shown openly to the nations. He has remembered his loving kindness and faithfulness toward the house of Israel, and all the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of God. The psalm summons all the earth to joyful noise with harp, voice, trumpets, and ram's horn before the King, and calls the sea, the world, the rivers, and the mountains to join in. The reason given is that the LORD comes to judge the earth with righteousness and the peoples with equity.

The LORD has done marvelous things, and his right hand and holy arm have worked salvation for him. He has made known his salvation, shown his righteousness to the nations, and remembered his loving kindness and faithfulness toward the house of Israel. He is called the King and is said to come to judge the earth and the world with righteousness and the peoples with equity.

l: all the earth (the inhabitants of the earth), Psalms, Chapter 98
s: All the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of God. The earth is told to make a joyful noise, burst out and sing for joy, and sing praises with harp, voice, trumpets, and ram's horn. The sea, the world and those who dwell in it, the rivers, and the mountains are also called to roar, clap, and sing before the LORD.

The LORD's right hand and holy arm have worked salvation for him. He has made it known and openly shown his righteousness in the sight of the nations. All the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of God.

l: new song (song to the LORD), Psalms, Chapter 98
s: The psalm opens by commanding that a new song be sung to the LORD because he has done marvelous things. Praise is to be given with joyful noise, the harp and the voice of melody, trumpets, and the ram's horn before the King.

l: judgment (the LORD's coming judgment), Psalms, Chapter 98
s: The LORD is said to be coming to judge the earth, and this is the reason creation is to sing before him. He will judge the world with righteousness and the peoples with equity.

Chapter 99 praises the LORD as the reigning king who sits enthroned among the cherubim and is great in Zion, high above all peoples. It says his strength loves justice, and that he establishes equity and executes justice and righteousness in Jacob. The people are called to exalt the LORD their God and worship at his footstool and holy hill, and the refrain declares that he is holy. The psalm recalls Moses, Aaron, and Samuel, who called on the LORD and were answered, with the LORD speaking to them in the pillar of cloud. It adds that the LORD forgave them while also taking vengeance for their doings.

The LORD reigns, enthroned among the cherubim, great in Zion and high above all peoples, and is repeatedly declared holy. He loves justice, establishes equity, and executes justice and righteousness in Jacob. He answered Moses, Aaron, and Samuel, spoke to them in the pillar of cloud, and forgave them although he took vengeance for their doings.

Moses is named as one of the LORD's priests who called on him, and the LORD answered. He and the others kept the LORD's testimonies and the statute given to them after the LORD spoke in the pillar of cloud.

Aaron is named alongside Moses as one of the LORD's priests who called on him and was answered. He kept the testimonies and statute the LORD gave, and was forgiven by God although vengeance was taken for his doings.
Samuel is described as among those who call on the LORD's name, and the LORD answered him. He is grouped with those to whom the LORD spoke and who kept his testimonies and statute.

Chapter 100 is a psalm of thanksgiving that calls all the lands to shout for joy to the LORD and to serve him with gladness and singing. It declares that the LORD is God, that he made us, and that we are his people and the sheep of his pasture. It then urges worshippers to enter his gates with thanksgiving and his courts with praise, giving thanks and blessing his name. It closes by stating that the LORD is good, that his loving kindness endures forever, and that his faithfulness lasts to all generations.

The LORD is called to be praised with joy, gladness, and singing, and is declared to be God, the one who made us. He is described as having a pasture with sheep, and as good, with loving kindness that endures forever and faithfulness to all generations.

All the lands are addressed directly and commanded to shout for joy to the LORD. Together with the other worshippers, they are urged to serve him with gladness and to come before his presence with singing.

The people are identified as belonging to the LORD, who made them: "we are his." They are called his people and the sheep of his pasture, and they are urged to enter his gates and courts with thanksgiving and praise.

Thanksgiving and praise are the prescribed manner of approaching the LORD, with worshippers entering his gates with thanksgiving and his courts with praise. They are also to give thanks to him and bless his name, because he is good and his loving kindness and faithfulness endure.

Chapter 101 is a psalm attributed to David in which the speaker vows to sing of loving kindness and justice to the LORD. He resolves to live a blameless life, at home and in his dealings, rejecting vile things, perverse hearts, slander, arrogance, deceit, and falsehood. He promises to favor the faithful of the land, letting them dwell with him and serve him. He closes by vowing to destroy all the wicked of the land each morning and cut off the workers of iniquity from the LORD's city.
David is named as the author of this psalm. The psalm expresses commitments to justice, blamelessness, and the removal of wickedness.
The LORD is the one to whom the speaker sings praises and whose coming he asks about. The city in which the speaker plans to cut off the workers of iniquity is called the LORD's city.

The speaker vows to sing of loving kindness and justice and to walk blamelessly in his house. He pledges to set no vile thing before his eyes, silence slanderers, tolerate no arrogant person, and keep the deceitful and false from his house and sight. He favors the faithful as servants and resolves to destroy the wicked of the land every morning.

l: the wicked of the land, Psalms, Chapter 101
s: The wicked of the land, also described as workers of iniquity, are the target of the speaker's resolve. He says he will destroy them morning by morning and cut them off from the LORD's city.

l: loving kindness and justice, Psalms, Chapter 101
s: Loving kindness and justice are the subjects of the speaker's song, which he sings as praise to the LORD.
A blameless life is something the speaker resolves to live carefully, with a blameless heart within his house. He also says that those who walk in a perfect way will serve him.

Chapter 102 is the prayer of an afflicted person who pours out his complaint before the LORD. He pleads for a quick answer, describes his wasting body, loss of appetite, loneliness, and mocking enemies, and attributes his state to the LORD's indignation and wrath. He then turns to the LORD's everlasting renown and the coming time to have mercy on Zion, when nations and kings will fear the LORD's name and a future people will praise him for hearing the prisoner and the condemned. The speaker returns to his own weakened strength and shortened days, asks God not to take him away mid-life, and contrasts the perishing heavens and earth with the unchanging LORD, ending with confidence that the servants' children will continue established before him.

The LORD is petitioned to hear, not hide his face, and answer quickly, and is said to have thrown the speaker away in indignation and wrath and to have weakened his strength and shortened his days. He remains forever, will arise and have mercy on Zion, has built it up and appeared in glory, has responded to the destitute's prayer, looked down from his sanctuary to hear the prisoner's groans and free the condemned, and will be praised by nations and a future people.

The speaker cries out in distress, describing days consumed like smoke, burned bones, a withered heart, forgotten food, lonely watching like a sparrow on a housetop, and enemies who reproach him and use his name as a curse. He ends by asking God not to take him away in the middle of his days and affirms that the children of God's servants will continue.

Zion is the object of the LORD's coming mercy, for the set time to pity her has come, and the LORD's servants take pleasure in her stones and pity her dust. The LORD has built her up and appeared in glory, and men will declare his name in Zion and praise in Jerusalem when peoples and kingdoms gather to serve him.

l: psalmist's distress and complaint, Psalms, Chapter 102
s: The distress is expressed in images of smoke, burning bones, withered grass, groaning, loneliness as a pelican, owl, and sparrow, eating ashes like bread, and mixing drink with tears. It is attributed to the LORD's indignation and wrath, and the speaker brings it before him as a prayer for a quick answer, noting that his strength and days have been cut short.

l: God's eternity versus human transience, Psalms, Chapter 102
s: The speaker's days are likened to a long shadow and withering grass, while the LORD remains forever and his renown endures to all generations. The earth's foundations and the heavens, God's own works, will perish and wear out like a garment, but God is the same and his years have no end, and the servants' children will be established before him.

Chapter 103, attributed to David, is a psalm in which the speaker calls on his own soul to praise the LORD and not forget his benefits. The LORD is described as forgiving sins, healing diseases, redeeming life, and satisfying desires, and as merciful, gracious, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness. His compassion toward those who fear him is compared to a father's toward his children, and his removal of transgressions to the distance between east and west. Human life is contrasted as brief, like grass or a flower, while the LORD's loving kindness is from everlasting to everlasting. The psalm ends with a call for angels, armies, servants, and all his works to praise the LORD, and a final self-address to David's soul.

The LORD is praised for forgiving sins, healing diseases, redeeming life, crowning with loving kindness, and satisfying desires with good things. He executes righteous acts and justice for the oppressed, made his ways known to Moses and his deeds to the children of Israel, and is merciful, gracious, slow to anger, and has not dealt with us according to our sins. He knows that we are dust, has established his throne in the heavens, and his kingdom rules over all.

David's soul is addressed repeatedly and told to praise the LORD's holy name with all that is within him. It is urged not to forget the LORD's benefits, and the psalm closes by again telling it to praise the LORD.

l: those who fear him, Psalms, Chapter 103
s: Those who fear the LORD receive loving kindness as great as the heavens are high above the earth. The LORD has compassion on them as a father has on his children, and his loving kindness is from everlasting to everlasting with them, with his righteousness extending to their children's children.

l: LORD's loving kindness and mercy, Psalms, Chapter 103
s: The LORD is described as abundant in loving kindness, and he crowns the speaker with loving kindness and tender mercies. His loving kindness toward those who fear him is as high as the heavens above the earth, and it lasts from everlasting to everlasting.
The LORD is said to forgive all sins and not to deal with us according to our sins or repay us for our iniquities. He has removed our transgressions from us as far as the east is from the west.

Chapter 104 is a psalm in which the speaker blesses the LORD for his greatness and for the work of creation. The LORD is described as clothed in light and majesty, laying the earth's foundations, covering it with the deep, and then setting boundaries so the waters would not return. He sends springs, grass, plants, wine, oil, bread, and trees to sustain wild animals, livestock, birds, and people. The psalm depicts the rhythm of day and night, the sea with its ships and leviathan, and the dependence of every creature on the LORD for food, breath, and renewal. The speaker vows to sing to the LORD for life, asks that his meditation be sweet to him, and asks that sinners and the wicked be consumed from the earth.

The LORD is praised as very great, clothed with honor, majesty, and light, who stretches out the heavens, rides the clouds and wind, and lays the earth's foundations. He rebuked the waters, assigned the mountains and valleys their places, set a boundary for the waters, and supplies springs, plants, and food for all creatures. He gives and withdraws breath, sends out his Spirit to create and renew the ground, and is asked to let his glory endure and to rejoice in his works.

The speaker calls on his own soul to bless the LORD and addresses him in praise throughout. He vows to sing to the LORD as long as he lives, asks that his meditation be sweet to him, and says he will rejoice in the LORD. He also asks that sinners be consumed out of the earth and the wicked be no more.

The earth was founded by the LORD so that it should not be moved forever, and was once covered by the deep with waters standing above the mountains. At the LORD's rebuke the waters fled, the mountains rose and the valleys sank, and a boundary now keeps the waters from covering it again. It is watered, filled with the fruit of the LORD's works and riches, and trembles when he looks at it.

Wild donkeys, birds, livestock, wild goats, rock badgers, storks, and forest animals are shown drinking from the springs, nesting in trees, and finding refuge in the high mountains and rocks. Young lions roar after prey and seek their food from God, then lie down in their dens at sunrise. In the sea, innumerable small and large creatures and leviathan live, and all wait on the LORD for food, are satisfied when he opens his hand, and die when he takes away their breath.

The psalm presents creation as the LORD's wise work and ongoing provision: springs and rain, grass for livestock, plants, wine, oil, and bread for man, and trees for birds. The moon and sun mark seasons and the cycle of night and day, in which animals prowl and man labors. All creatures depend on him for food in due season, and he renews the face of the ground by sending out his Spirit.

Chapter 105 is a psalm calling Israel, the offspring of Abraham and children of Jacob, to give thanks to the LORD and remember his marvelous works. It recounts how the LORD remembered his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, promising the land of Canaan when they were few and wandering as foreigners, and protecting them from kings. It tells how he sent Joseph, sold as a slave and imprisoned, who was freed by the king and made ruler of his house. Israel then came into Egypt, grew strong, and was hated by the Egyptians, so the LORD sent Moses and Aaron, who performed wonders and plagues, and he brought his people out with silver and gold. The psalm ends with the LORD's provision in the wilderness, the gift of the nations' lands, and the purpose that they keep his statutes.

The LORD is called on to be thanked and sought, and is described as remembering his covenant forever and protecting his people, even reproving kings for their sakes. He sent Joseph ahead, turned the Egyptians' hearts against his people, sent Moses and Aaron, struck Egypt with plagues, brought his people out, and provided cloud, fire, quail, and water from the rock. He gave them the lands of the nations so they might keep his statutes.

Abraham is called the LORD's servant, and his offspring are urged to remember the LORD's works. The LORD made a covenant with him, and remembering his holy word and Abraham is why the LORD brought his people out.
Jacob is named as one whose children are the LORD's chosen ones. The LORD confirmed the covenant to him as a statute, and Jacob lived in the land of Ham when Israel came into Egypt.

Israel is confirmed an everlasting covenant and promised the land of Canaan. Israel came into Egypt, was increased greatly and made stronger than its adversaries, was hated by the Egyptians, and was then brought out with joy and singing. Israel received the lands of the nations so that it might keep the LORD's statutes and laws.

Joseph was sent by the LORD before his people, was sold as a slave, and was bound with shackles and irons. After his word proved true, the king freed him and made him lord of his house and ruler of all his possessions, to discipline princes and teach elders wisdom.
Moses is called the LORD's servant, sent along with Aaron, whom the LORD had chosen. They performed miracles and wonders among the Egyptians in the land of Ham.

Egypt is called the land of Ham, where Jacob lived and Israel increased. It suffered darkness, blood-filled waters, frogs, flies, lice, hail, locusts, and the death of its firstborn. Egypt was glad when the people departed because fear of them had fallen on it.

l: Egyptian enemies (adversaries at the Red Sea), Psalms, Chapter 105
s: The Egyptians had their hearts turned by the LORD to hate his people and conspire against his servants. They did not rebel against his words of darkness, and they suffered the plagues. They were glad when Israel left, since fear of them had fallen on them.
Canaan is the land the LORD promised to give Israel as the lot of their inheritance. The promise was made when the patriarchs were few in number and foreigners in it.

l: covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, Psalms, Chapter 105
s: The LORD has remembered this covenant forever, the word he commanded to a thousand generations. It was made with Abraham, sworn as an oath to Isaac, and confirmed to Jacob and Israel as an everlasting covenant, with the promise of the land of Canaan.

The LORD sent darkness, turned the waters into blood and killed the fish, and sent frogs, flies, lice, hail with lightning, and locusts and grasshoppers. Hail struck vines and fig trees, locusts ate every plant and fruit, and the LORD struck all the firstborn in the land.

The LORD brought his people out with silver and gold, and not one feeble person was among the tribes. Egypt was glad at their departure, and the LORD covered them with a cloud and gave fire at night. He provided quails, bread of the sky, and water from the opened rock, bringing his chosen out with joy and singing.

Psalm 106 opens with praise of the LORD for his goodness and enduring loving kindness, and the psalmist asks to be remembered with salvation for his people. The psalm then confesses that the Israelites sinned together with their fathers, recounting rebellion at the Red Sea, craving in the desert, envy of Moses and Aaron, the golden calf at Horeb, despising the pleasant land, worship of Baal Peor, and the trouble at Meribah. It also recounts that they mixed with the nations, served idols, sacrificed their sons and daughters to demons, and polluted the land with blood. In response the LORD burned with anger and gave them to the nations, yet he repeatedly rescued them, heard their cry, and remembered his covenant. The psalm closes with a plea to be gathered from among the nations and a blessing of the LORD, the God of Israel.

The LORD is praised as good, with loving kindness that endures forever, and he saved the fathers at the Red Sea for his name's sake to make his power known. He punished their rebellion, including the earth swallowing Dathan, fire burning the wicked, a plague, and giving them into the hand of the nations. Yet he regarded their distress, remembered his covenant, repented according to his loving kindnesses, and made their captors pity them.

l: Israelites (the fathers and their offspring), Psalms, Chapter 106
s: The Israelites confess that they sinned with their fathers, who forgot God's wonders, rebelled at the Red Sea, craved in the desert, made a calf, murmured in their tents, joined Baal Peor, mixed with the nations and sacrificed their children to idols. As a result they were ruled and oppressed by their enemies and brought low in iniquity, but God heard their cry and remembered his covenant. The psalmist prays that God will save them and gather them from among the nations.

Moses is described as God's chosen, whom the people envied in the camp. He stood before God in the breach to turn away his wrath so that God would not destroy the people. At the waters of Meribah, the people's rebellion troubled him and he spoke rashly with his lips.

At the Red Sea the fathers were rebellious, not understanding God's wonders. God rebuked it and it dried up, leading them through the depths as through a desert, and its waters covered their adversaries so that none was left. The Red Sea is also named among the sites of God's awesome works.
The fathers made a calf in Horeb and worshiped it as a molten image. By doing so they exchanged their glory for the image of a bull that eats grass, forgetting God their Savior.

l: Israel's repeated rebellion and God's mercy, Psalms, Chapter 106
s: The psalm sets out a pattern in which the people believe and sing praise, then soon forget God's works and rebel, as at the Red Sea, in the desert, at Horeb, at Baal Peor, at Meribah and in Canaan. Each time God judges them but also saves, finally regarding their distress and remembering his covenant according to his loving kindnesses. The psalm says he rescued them many times, though they were rebellious in their counsel.

Chapter 107 calls the redeemed of the LORD to give thanks for his enduring loving kindness. It describes four groups in distress who cry to the LORD and are delivered: wanderers in the wilderness who were hungry and thirsty, prisoners in darkness who had rebelled against God, fools afflicted by their disobedience who neared the gates of death, and seafarers caught in a storm. After each rescue the refrain urges them to praise the LORD for his wonderful deeds. The chapter then says the LORD turns rivers and fruitful land into desert and salt waste because of wickedness, and turns desert into pools and springs where the hungry build a city, sow fields, and multiply. It ends by saying the LORD lifts the needy and humbles princes, the upright rejoice, the wicked are silenced, and the wise should consider his loving kindnesses.

The LORD hears the cries of the wanderers, prisoners, fools, and seafarers and delivers each from their distress. He breaks gates of bronze and bars of iron, sends his word to heal, calms the storm, and turns deserts into water springs and fruitful land into salt waste. He also pours contempt on princes and lifts the needy, and he is to be praised for his loving kindness and wonderful deeds.

l: the redeemed (redeemed by the LORD), Psalms, Chapter 107
s: The redeemed are called to give thanks and say so, having been redeemed from the hand of the adversary. They are described as gathered out of the lands from east, west, north, and south.

l: wanderers in the wilderness (gathered from the lands), Psalms, Chapter 107
s: They wandered in a desert way, found no city to live in, and were hungry and thirsty until their soul fainted. They cried to the LORD, who delivered them and led them by a straight way to a city to live in. They are told to praise him because he satisfies the longing soul and fills the hungry with good.

l: prisoners in darkness (those who rebelled against God), Psalms, Chapter 107
s: They sat in darkness and the shadow of death, bound in affliction and iron, because they rebelled against God's words and condemned the counsel of the Most High. Their hearts were brought down with labor and no one helped, but when they cried to the LORD he saved them, brought them out, and broke their chains. He broke the gates of bronze and cut the bars of iron for them.

Fools are afflicted because of their disobedience and iniquities, so that their soul abhors all food and they draw near the gates of death. When they cry to the LORD, he saves them, sending his word to heal them and deliver them from their graves. They are urged to offer sacrifices of thanksgiving and declare his deeds with singing.

l: seafarers (those who go down to the sea in ships), Psalms, Chapter 107
s: Seafarers who do business in great waters see the LORD's deeds and wonders in the deep. When he raises a stormy wind they mount to the sky and sink to the depths, reel like drunken men, and reach their wits' end. They cry to him, he stills the storm, and he brings them to their desired haven, and they are urged to exalt him in the assembly and among the elders.

The LORD's loving kindness is said to endure forever and is the reason given for thanks and praise after each deliverance. The chapter ends by telling the wise to pay attention and consider the LORD's loving kindnesses.

l: desert and fruitful land (transformed land), Psalms, Chapter 107
s: The LORD turns rivers into desert, water springs into thirsty ground, and fruitful land into a salt waste because of the wickedness of those who dwell there. He also turns desert into a pool of water and dry land into springs, where the hungry live, prepare a city, sow fields, plant vineyards, and reap increase.

Chapter 108 is a psalm attributed to David in which the speaker declares a steadfast heart and resolves to sing and make music, waking the dawn with harp and lyre. The speaker vows to give thanks and praise to the LORD among the nations and peoples, because God's loving kindness is great above the heavens and his faithfulness reaches the skies. The speaker asks God to be exalted above the heavens and to save his beloved with his right hand. God is then quoted as speaking from his sanctuary, claiming Shechem, Succoth, Gilead, Manasseh, Ephraim, and Judah, and declaring Moab his wash pot, with a sandal tossed on Edom and a shout over Philistia. The psalm closes with a question about who will lead the speaker to the fortified city and Edom, a lament that God has rejected his people and does not go out with their armies, and a plea for help against the enemy, trusting that through God they will do valiantly.

God is addressed as the one whose loving kindness is great above the heavens and whose faithfulness reaches the skies, and the speaker asks that he be exalted above the heavens with glory over all the earth. He speaks from his sanctuary, claiming Shechem, Succoth, Gilead, Manasseh, Ephraim, and Judah, and declaring dominion over Moab, Edom, and Philistia. The speaker laments that God has rejected his people and does not go out with their armies, yet trusts that through him they will do valiantly and he will tread down their enemies.
David is named in the superscription as the one to whom this song and psalm is attributed. The text says nothing else about him in this unit.

The speaker declares a steadfast heart, resolves to sing and make music with his soul, and calls on harp and lyre to wake so that he may wake the dawn. He vows to thank and praise the LORD among the nations and peoples, and asks God to save his beloved and answer. He also laments that God has rejected the people, asks who will lead him to the fortified city and to Edom, pleads for help against the enemy, and expresses confidence that through God they will do valiantly.
The beloved are those the speaker asks God to deliver by saving with his right hand and answering. The request is made so that they may be delivered.
The enemies are the adversary against whom the speaker asks God for help, since the help of man is vain. The speaker expresses confidence that God will tread them down.

l: loving kindness and faithfulness (God's), Psalms, Chapter 108
s: God's loving kindness is described as great above the heavens, and his faithfulness as reaching to the skies. These attributes are the stated reason for the speaker's thanks and praise among the nations.

The speaker resolves to give thanks to the LORD among the nations and to sing praises to him among the peoples. This is accompanied by singing, music with the soul, and the waking of harp and lyre and of the dawn.

Chapter 109 is a psalm by David for the Chief Musician in which he asks God not to stay silent while enemies attack him with lying words and hatred, repaying his love with evil. He then calls down a long series of curses on a wicked man: a wicked man set over him, a guilty verdict, few days, fatherless children, plundered goods, and his name blotted out, because that man showed no kindness, persecuted the poor and needy, and loved cursing. David describes himself as poor, needy, wounded, faint from fasting, and mocked by those who shake their heads. He asks the LORD to help and save him according to his loving kindness so that all will know it is the LORD's hand. He ends by asking that his adversaries be clothed with shame, and promises to give great thanks and praise the LORD, who stands at the right hand of the needy.

The LORD is addressed as the God of David's praise and asked not to be silent, to deal with David for his name's sake, and to save him according to his loving kindness. He is asked to remember the iniquity of the wicked man's fathers and to cut off the memory of the wicked man's family from the earth. David says the LORD blesses where others curse and stands at the right hand of the needy to save them from those who judge his soul.

David, author of the psalm, prays against adversaries who speak lies and hatred against him without cause and repay his love with evil. He describes himself as poor, needy, heart-wounded, weak from fasting, thin, and a reproach to others. He asks the LORD for help and rescue and vows to give great thanks and praise him among the multitude.

David's adversaries open wicked and deceitful mouths against him, surround him with words of hatred, fight him without cause, and repay his love with hostility and evil for good. They shake their heads at him in scorn. David asks that they be clothed with dishonor and covered with their own shame as with a robe, and says they will be shamed when they arise.

l: wicked man (David's chief adversary), Psalms, Chapter 109
s: The wicked man is the target of David's detailed curses: an adversary set over him, a guilty verdict, a prayer turned to sin, few days, loss of his office, a widowed wife, beggar children, plundered possessions, and a name blotted out. The reasons given are that he showed no kindness, persecuted the poor, needy, and broken-hearted to kill them, and loved cursing, which clothed him like a garment and soaked into him like water and oil.

l: Psalm 109 (curse on the adversary), Psalms, Chapter 109
s: In this unit the psalm opens with a complaint about lying enemies, moves into an extended series of curses on a wicked man and his family in verses 6-19, and declares in verse 20 that this is the LORD's reward to David's adversaries. It then turns to David's own plea and ends with a vow of thanks and praise.

David asks the LORD to deliver him for his name's sake and because his loving kindness is good, citing his poverty, wounded heart, fading strength, and weakness from fasting. He says he wants the rescue to show that it is the LORD's hand, and he is confident that the LORD will stand at the right hand of the needy to save him. He promises great thanks and public praise in return.

Chapter 110 is a psalm of David in which the LORD addresses David's Lord, telling him to sit at his right hand until the enemies are made a footstool for his feet. The LORD will send the rod of his strength out of Zion and has him rule among his enemies. His people offer themselves willingly in holy array on the day of his power. The LORD swears an unchangeable oath that he is a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek. The Lord at the LORD's right hand will crush kings in the day of his wrath, judge among the nations, heap up dead bodies, and crush the ruler of the whole earth, then drink from the brook on the way and lift up his head.

The LORD tells David's Lord to sit at his right hand until the enemies are made his footstool. He will send out the rod of his strength out of Zion. He swears an oath he will not change his mind about, declaring that David's Lord is a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.

David's Lord is told to sit at the LORD's right hand and to rule among his enemies. His people offer themselves willingly in holy array on the day of his power, and he is declared a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek. He will crush kings in the day of his wrath, judge among the nations, heap up dead bodies, and crush the ruler of the whole earth. He will drink from the brook on the way and therefore lift up his head.

The enemies are to be made a footstool for the feet of David's Lord, who is to rule among them. Kings and the ruler of the whole earth are to be crushed in the day of his wrath, and dead bodies will be heaped up among the nations.

Chapter 111 is a psalm of praise in which the speaker gives thanks to the LORD with his whole heart among the upright and in the congregation. It describes the LORD's works as great, honorable, majestic, true and just, and says his righteousness endures forever. The LORD is gracious and merciful, gives food to those who fear him, remembers his covenant, and has given his people the heritage of the nations. He has sent redemption to his people and ordained his covenant forever, and his name is holy and awesome. The psalm closes by saying the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom and that those who do his work have good understanding.

The LORD is praised and thanked with the speaker's whole heart. He is described as gracious and merciful, righteous forever, and holy and awesome in name. He gives food to those who fear him, remembers his covenant, gives his people the heritage of the nations, sends redemption, and ordains his covenant forever.

l: those who trust in the LORD (the LORD's people), Psalms, Chapter 111
s: The LORD's people are shown the power of his works and are given the heritage of the nations. He has sent redemption to them and ordained his covenant forever.

l: works of the LORD, Psalms, Chapter 111
s: The LORD's works are called great, pondered by all who delight in them, and characterized by honor and majesty. They are described as truth and justice, with all his precepts sure and established forever and ever, done in truth and uprightness. He has caused his wonderful works to be remembered.
Wisdom is said to have its beginning in the fear of the LORD. Those who do his work are said to have a good understanding.

l: fear of the LORD, Psalms, Chapter 111
s: The fear of the LORD is declared the beginning of wisdom. Those who fear him are the ones to whom the LORD gives food.

Chapter 112 opens with praise to the LORD and describes the blessings of the man who fears the LORD and delights in his commandments. His offspring will be mighty, his house will hold wealth and riches, and his righteousness endures forever. He is gracious, merciful, and generous, lending and giving to the poor, and he will never be shaken or afraid of evil news because his heart trusts in the LORD. He will see his adversaries without fear, and his horn will be exalted with honor. The wicked see this and are grieved, gnashing their teeth and melting away, and their desire will perish.
The LORD is praised at the opening of the chapter. He is the one whom the blessed man fears and in whom that man's steadfast heart trusts, and his commandments are what the man delights in greatly.

l: the man who fears the LORD, Psalms, Chapter 112
s: The man who fears the LORD is called blessed, delights greatly in the LORD's commandments, and is gracious, merciful, and righteous. He deals graciously, lends, and gives to the poor. His offspring will be mighty, wealth and riches are in his house, and his righteousness endures forever. He will never be shaken, will be remembered forever, will not fear evil news, will not fear when he sees his adversaries, and will have his horn exalted with honor.
The wicked will see the blessing and honor of the man who fears the LORD and be grieved. They will gnash their teeth and melt away, and their desire will perish.

Chapter 113 is a hymn of praise to the LORD. It calls the servants of the LORD to praise his name now and forever, from sunrise to sunset. It declares the LORD high above all nations and above the heavens, with no one like him, as he stoops down to see heaven and earth. It describes him raising the poor from the dust and the needy from the ash heap to sit with princes of his people. It ends with him settling the barren woman in her home as a joyful mother of children.

The LORD is praised from this time forward and forever, from sunrise to sunset. He is high above all nations with glory above the heavens, has his seat on high, and stoops down to see in heaven and on earth. He raises the poor and needy and settles the barren woman in her home as a joyful mother.

l: servants of the LORD, Psalms, Chapter 113
s: The servants of the LORD are called on to praise the LORD's name. The psalm opens with this command and frames their praise as fitting from this time forward and forever.
The LORD raises the poor out of the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap. He sets him with princes, even the princes of his people.
The LORD settles the barren woman in her home. She becomes a joyful mother of children.

Chapter 114 celebrates the time when Israel, the house of Jacob, went out of Egypt from a people of foreign language. Judah became God's sanctuary and Israel his dominion. In response, the sea fled, the Jordan was driven back, and the mountains and little hills skipped like rams and lambs. The speaker asks why they did so, then commands the earth to tremble at the presence of the Lord, the God of Jacob, who turned the rock into a pool of water and the flint into a spring of waters.
Israel, also called the house of Jacob, went out of Egypt from a people of foreign language. It became God's dominion.
Egypt is the land Israel went out of. Its people are described as a people of foreign language.
Judah became God's sanctuary when Israel went out of Egypt.

The Lord, the God of Jacob, is the one before whom the earth is told to tremble. He turned the rock into a pool of water and the flint into a spring of waters. Judah became his sanctuary and Israel his dominion.
The sea saw it and fled. It is then asked why it fled.
The Jordan was driven back, or turned back. It is then asked why it turned back.
The mountains skipped like rams. They are asked what caused them to do so.
The little hills skipped like lambs. They are asked why they did so.

The going out of Israel from Egypt, from a people of foreign language, is the event that begins the chapter. Judah became God's sanctuary and Israel his dominion, and the sea, Jordan, mountains and hills reacted to it.

In Chapter 115 the speaker asks the LORD to give glory to his own name rather than to the people, for the sake of his loving kindness and truth, and asks why the nations should say 'Where is their God?'. The chapter contrasts the LORD, who is in the heavens and does whatever he pleases, with the idols of the nations, which are silver and gold, made by human hands, and unable to speak, see, hear, smell, feel or walk. It says that those who make idols and trust in them will be like them. Israel, the house of Aaron, and those who fear the LORD are each called to trust in the LORD as their help and shield, and are promised his blessing and increase. The chapter closes by noting that the heavens belong to the LORD while the earth is given to humans, that the dead do not praise him, and that the speakers will bless him forever.

The LORD is asked to give glory to his name for the sake of his loving kindness and truth. He is in the heavens, does whatever he pleases, and is the help and shield of Israel, the house of Aaron, and those who fear him. He remembers and will bless them, small and great, made heaven and earth, keeps the heavens as his own, and has given the earth to the children of men.
Israel is exhorted to trust in the LORD, who is their help and shield. The LORD will bless the house of Israel.
The house of Aaron is exhorted to trust in the LORD, who is their help and shield. The LORD will bless the house of Aaron.

l: those who fear the LORD, Psalms, Chapter 115
s: Those who fear the LORD are told to trust in him, as he is their help and shield. He will bless them, both small and great, and the speaker wishes that he would increase them and their children.

The idols are described as silver and gold, the work of men's hands. They have mouths, eyes, ears, noses, hands and feet but cannot speak, see, hear, smell, feel or walk. Those who make them and trust in them will become like them.

Chapter 116 is a psalmist's song of thanksgiving to the LORD for hearing his cries and delivering him from death, trouble, and sorrow. He recounts calling on the LORD's name when the cords of death and the pains of Sheol surrounded him, and says the LORD, who is gracious, righteous, and merciful, saved him. He tells his soul to return to rest, and resolves to walk before the LORD in the land of the living. He admits he said in haste that all people are liars, and asks what he can give the LORD for his benefits. He answers by vowing to take the cup of salvation, offer the sacrifice of thanksgiving, and pay his vows before all the LORD's people in the courts of the LORD's house in Jerusalem.

The LORD listens to the psalmist's voice and cries for mercy, turns his ear to him, and delivers his soul from death, his eyes from tears, and his feet from falling. He is described as gracious, righteous, and merciful, and as preserving the simple. The death of his saints is precious in his sight, and the psalmist vows to call on his name, pay vows, and offer thanksgiving in his house in Jerusalem.

The psalmist declares his love for the LORD because he was heard, and recounts being surrounded by the cords of death and the pains of Sheol before calling on the LORD's name and being saved. He calls himself the LORD's servant, the son of his servant girl, freed from chains, and admits he said in haste that all people are liars. He resolves to walk before the LORD, take the cup of salvation, offer the sacrifice of thanksgiving, and pay his vows publicly in the courts of the LORD's house in Jerusalem.

Chapter 117 is a two-verse psalm of praise addressed to all nations and all peoples. They are called to praise and extol the LORD. The stated reason is that the LORD's loving kindness toward 'us' is great and his faithfulness endures forever. The chapter closes by repeating the call: 'Praise the LORD!'
The LORD is the one whom all nations and peoples are commanded to praise and extol. He is described as having great loving kindness toward 'us' and faithfulness that endures forever.
All the nations, along with all peoples, are called on to praise the LORD and extol him. No response is recorded in this unit; it is only a summons.

l: loving kindness (the LORD's loving kindness), Psalms, Chapter 117
s: The LORD's loving kindness is said to be great toward 'us'. It is given as a reason for the nations and peoples to praise him.
The LORD's faithfulness is said to endure forever. It is given, together with his loving kindness, as grounds for praising him.

Chapter 118 is a psalm of thanksgiving that opens and closes by calling on all to give thanks to the LORD because he is good and his loving kindness endures forever. Israel, the house of Aaron, and those who fear the LORD are each summoned to repeat that refrain. The speaker recounts being in distress and answered by the LORD, then describes being surrounded by nations that he cut off in the LORD's name. He declares that he will live and declare the LORD's works, though the LORD punished him severely, and he enters the gates of righteousness to give thanks. The psalm celebrates the rejected stone becoming the cornerstone, the day the LORD made, and a blessing on the one who comes in the LORD's name, ending with the sacrifice bound to the altar's horns.

The LORD is described as good, with loving kindness that endures forever. He answered the speaker's call in distress, helped him, became his strength, song and salvation, punished him severely without giving him over to death, and gave light to the people.

Israel is called upon to say that the LORD's loving kindness endures forever, alongside the house of Aaron and those who fear the LORD. The text also gives voice to a group using 'us' and 'we', who celebrate the day the LORD made and ask him to save them.

The speaker called on the LORD out of distress and was answered with freedom, so he says he will not be afraid of man and will look in triumph at those who hate him. He was surrounded and pushed hard but was helped, and he vows to live, declare the LORD's works, enter the gates of righteousness and give thanks, calling the LORD his God whom he will exalt.
The nations surrounded the speaker on all sides, like bees. In the LORD's name the speaker cut them off, and they are said to be quenched like burning thorns.

Chapter 119 is a long acrostic poem in which a psalmist praises the LORD's law, statutes, precepts, and commandments across 22 lettered sections. The psalmist vows to obey, meditate on, and love the law, and repeatedly asks the LORD for teaching, understanding, and revival. He describes affliction, slander, and persecution from proud and wicked people, yet says he does not forsake the law. He affirms that the LORD's word is settled forever, is truth, and is a lamp to his feet and a light for his path. The chapter ends with the psalmist asking the LORD to hear his cry and save him, and confessing that he has gone astray like a lost sheep.

The LORD is addressed as the giver of commandments, statutes, and precepts, and is called righteous, good, faithful, and near. The psalmist asks him to teach, revive, redeem, and deliver him, and says the LORD has afflicted him in faithfulness, rebuked the proud, and put away the wicked like dross. His word is described as settled in heaven forever and his faithfulness as lasting to all generations.

The psalmist vows to keep, meditate on, delight in, and love the LORD's law with his whole heart, and prays repeatedly for teaching, understanding, and revival. He is afflicted, despised, and persecuted by princes and the proud, yet says he does not forget the law, rises at midnight and before dawn, and praises seven times a day. He ends by confessing that he has gone astray like a lost sheep and asking the LORD to seek him.

The law, also called statutes, precepts, commandments, testimonies, and ordinances, is presented as the path to a blameless and pure life and as the source of blessing, peace, and understanding. It is called a lamp to the psalmist's feet and a light for his path, sweeter than honey and better than gold and silver. It is described as truth, righteous, and enduring forever.

l: the proud and wicked (enemies of the psalmist), Psalms, Chapter 119
s: The proud and wicked slander, mock, and persecute the psalmist, dig pits and lay snares and ropes for him, and smear him with lies. They forsake and break the law and are far from it, and the psalmist feels indignation and sorrow over them. The LORD is said to have rebuked the proud, to reject those who stray, and to put away the wicked like dross, and the psalmist asks that the proud be disappointed.

Chapter 120 is a Song of Ascents in which the psalmist recounts crying to the LORD in distress and being answered. The speaker asks the LORD to deliver his soul from lying lips and a deceitful tongue, and asks what will be given and done to that deceitful tongue, answering with sharp arrows of the mighty and coals of juniper. He laments living in Meshech and dwelling among the tents of Kedar. He says his soul has dwelt too long with one who hates peace, and that although he is for peace, when he speaks, they are for war.
The LORD is the one to whom the speaker cried in distress, and He answered him. The speaker asks Him to deliver his soul from lying lips and a deceitful tongue.

The speaker cried to the LORD in distress, was answered, and asks to be delivered from lying lips and a deceitful tongue. He laments living in Meshech and dwelling among the tents of Kedar, and says his soul has lived too long with one who hates peace. He declares himself for peace, yet when he speaks, others are for war.

l: lying lips and deceitful tongue (the speaker's slanderers), Psalms, Chapter 120
s: The lying lips and deceitful tongue are what the speaker asks the LORD to deliver his soul from. The deceitful tongue is addressed directly and asked what will be given and done to it, with the answer being sharp arrows of the mighty and coals of juniper.

l: him who hates peace (the speaker's neighbor), Psalms, Chapter 120
s: He is the one with whom the speaker's soul has dwelt too long. He hates peace, and the speaker notes that when he speaks for peace, they are for war.

Chapter 121 is a Song of Ascents in which the speaker lifts his eyes to the hills and asks where his help comes from. The speaker answers that help comes from the LORD, who made heaven and earth. The psalm then describes the LORD as a keeper who will not let a foot be moved and who neither slumbers nor sleeps, and who keeps Israel. It promises that the LORD is a shade at the right hand, so that neither sun by day nor moon by night will cause harm. It closes by saying the LORD will keep from all evil, will keep the soul, and will keep going out and coming in from now and forever.

The LORD is identified as the source of the speaker's help and as the maker of heaven and earth. He is described as Israel's keeper who neither slumbers nor sleeps, as a shade at the right hand, and as the one who will keep from all evil, keep the soul, and keep going out and coming in forever.

Chapter 122 is a Song of Ascents attributed to David. The speaker recalls gladness when others said, "Let's go to the LORD's house," and rejoices that his feet now stand within Jerusalem's gates. He describes Jerusalem as a compactly built city where the LORD's tribes go up, by ordinance for Israel, to give thanks to the LORD's name, and where thrones of judgment belong to David's house. He urges prayer for Jerusalem's peace and blesses the city with peace and prosperity. He closes by vowing, for the sake of his brothers and companions and of the house of the LORD our God, to seek Jerusalem's good.

Jerusalem is the city whose gates the speaker stands within. It is described as built compact together, as the place where the tribes go up, and as the seat of judgment thrones belonging to David's house. The speaker calls for prayer for its peace, blesses it with peace within its walls and prosperity within its palaces, and vows to seek its good.

The LORD is the one to whose house the people go and to whose name the tribes go up to give thanks, according to an ordinance for Israel. He is called "our God" by the speaker, who seeks Jerusalem's good for the sake of his house.

l: house of the LORD (the LORD's house), Psalms, Chapter 122
s: The LORD's house is the destination people invite the speaker to visit, which makes him glad. At the end of the unit it is named as the reason the speaker will seek Jerusalem's good.
The tribes are called the LORD's tribes and are said to go up to Jerusalem according to an ordinance for Israel. They go to give thanks to the LORD's name.

The speaker, in a psalm attributed to David, is glad when invited to go to the LORD's house and now stands within Jerusalem's gates. He urges prayer for Jerusalem's peace, pronounces peace upon it for the sake of his brothers and companions, and resolves to seek its good for the sake of the house of the LORD our God.

Peace is what the speaker urges others to pray for on Jerusalem's behalf, with the promise that those who love the city will prosper. He wishes it within Jerusalem's walls and says to the city, "Peace be within you."

Chapter 123, a Song of Ascents, is a short prayer addressed to the LORD, who sits in the heavens. The speaker begins by lifting their eyes to him, then compares the speakers' gaze to that of servants and maids watching the hand of their master or mistress. The speakers, using "we" and "our," wait on the LORD, their God, until he has mercy on them. They plead twice for mercy because they have endured much contempt. They say their soul is exceedingly filled with the scoffing of those who are at ease and with the contempt of the proud.

The LORD is addressed as the one who sits in the heavens and as the God of the speakers. The speakers look to him as servants look to a master's hand, waiting until he has mercy on them, and they ask him twice for that mercy.

The speakers lift their eyes to the LORD and wait on him like servants watching a master's or mistress's hand. They plead for mercy because they have endured much contempt, and their soul is exceedingly filled with the scoffing of those at ease and the contempt of the proud.

l: those who are at ease, Psalms, Chapter 123
s: Those who are at ease are described as the source of scoffing that exceedingly fills the speakers' soul. They are named alongside the proud, whose contempt is also mentioned.

The speakers say they have endured much contempt, which is the reason they ask the LORD for mercy. It is also described as coming from the proud, and it fills their soul together with the scoffing of those at ease.
Mercy is what the speakers wait for from the LORD, looking to him until he grants it. They ask for it twice in verse 3, grounding the request in the contempt they have endured.

Chapter 124 is a Song of Ascents attributed to David. The speaker, voicing the community, declares that if the LORD had not been on their side when men rose up against them, they would have been swallowed alive and overwhelmed by waters. Israel is invited to say this aloud. The LORD is blessed for not giving them as prey to their enemies' teeth, and the people's escape is pictured as a bird freed from a broken fowler's snare. The chapter ends by affirming that their help is in the LORD's name, who made heaven and earth.

The LORD is credited as the one who was on the side of the speakers when men rose up against them. He is blessed for not giving them as prey to their enemies' teeth, and the snare was broken so they escaped. He is named as the source of help and as the maker of heaven and earth.

Israel is called on to say that had the LORD not been on their side, they would have been swallowed alive and overwhelmed by waters. The community speaks as having escaped like a bird from a fowler's snare. They affirm that their help is in the LORD's name.

l: men (those who rose up against us), Psalms, Chapter 124
s: Men rose up against the speakers, and their wrath was kindled against them. Had the LORD not been on the speakers' side, these men would have swallowed them alive, but they were not allowed to make the speakers their prey. The speakers escaped and the snare was broken.

Chapter 125 is a Song of Ascents about the security of those who trust in the LORD. They are compared to Mount Zion, which cannot be moved, and the LORD surrounds them as mountains surround Jerusalem. The scepter of wickedness will not remain over the allotment of the righteous, so the righteous will not turn their hands to evil. The psalmist asks the LORD to do good to the good and upright in heart, while those who turn to crooked ways will be led away by the LORD with the workers of iniquity. The chapter closes with a blessing of peace on Israel.

The LORD surrounds his people from now and forever, as the mountains surround Jerusalem. He is asked to do good to those who are good and upright in heart, and he will lead away those who turn to crooked ways together with the workers of iniquity.
Mount Zion is the image of stability: it cannot be moved but remains forever. Those who trust in the LORD are compared to it.
Jerusalem is said to be surrounded by mountains. This serves as the comparison for how the LORD surrounds his people now and forever.

l: those who trust in the LORD (the LORD's people), Psalms, Chapter 125
s: They are likened to Mount Zion, immovable and enduring forever. The LORD surrounds them from this time forward and forever more.

The righteous have an allotment over which the scepter of wickedness will not remain. This is so that they will not use their hands to do evil. The psalmist asks the LORD to do good to the good and upright in heart.

l: the wicked (workers of iniquity), Psalms, Chapter 125
s: Those who turn away to their crooked ways will be led away by the LORD together with the workers of iniquity. The scepter of wickedness will not remain over the allotment of the righteous.

Chapter 126, a Song of Ascents, recalls the time when the LORD brought back those who returned to Zion, an experience so wondrous that they felt as though they were dreaming. Their mouths filled with laughter and singing, and the nations acknowledged that the LORD had done great things for them, which the speakers affirm and say makes them glad. The speakers then ask the LORD to restore their fortunes again, like the streams in the Negev. The psalm closes with the assurance that those who sow in tears will reap in joy, and that he who goes out weeping carrying seed will certainly return with joy carrying his sheaves.

The LORD is said to have brought back those who returned to Zion and to have done great things for them, which even the nations acknowledged. The speakers, glad at what he has done, ask him to restore their fortunes again like the streams in the Negev.
Zion is the place to which the LORD brought back those who returned, an event so astonishing that they felt like dreamers.

l: those who returned to Zion, Psalms, Chapter 126
s: Those who returned to Zion were brought back by the LORD and felt like those who dream. Their mouths filled with laughter and their tongues with singing, and the nations said the LORD had done great things for them.

The restoration of fortunes is the subject of a petition asking the LORD to restore them again, like the streams in the Negev. It is set against the earlier return to Zion, which the speakers remember as a great deed of the LORD.

l: those who sow in tears, Psalms, Chapter 126
s: Those who sow in tears are promised that they will reap in joy. The one who goes out weeping carrying seed for sowing will certainly come again with joy, carrying his sheaves.

Chapter 127 is a Song of Ascents attributed to Solomon. It declares that unless the LORD builds the house or watches over the city, the builders and the watchman labor in vain. It says rising early and staying up late to eat the bread of toil is vain, because the LORD gives sleep to his loved ones. It then calls children a heritage and reward from the LORD, likens the children of youth to arrows in a mighty man's hand, and pronounces happy the man whose quiver is full of them, who will not be disappointed when speaking with enemies in the gate.

The LORD is the one who must build the house and watch over the city, or the work of builders and watchmen is in vain. He gives sleep to his loved ones. Children are described as his heritage and reward.

Children are called a heritage of the LORD and the fruit of the womb is his reward. The children of youth are compared to arrows in the hand of a mighty man. A man who has a quiver full of them is called happy.

l: man (who has a full quiver), Psalms, Chapter 127
s: The man who has his quiver full of children is declared happy. He and his children will not be disappointed when they speak with their enemies in the gate.

l: vain labor and toil, Psalms, Chapter 127
s: Building the house and guarding the city are in vain unless the LORD builds and watches. Rising early, staying up late, and eating the bread of toil are likewise called vain, since the LORD gives sleep to his loved ones.

Chapter 128 is a Song of Ascents that declares blessed everyone who fears the LORD and walks in his ways. Such a person will eat the labor of his hands, be happy, and have things go well with him. His wife is likened to a fruitful vine in the innermost parts of his house, and his children to olive shoots around his table. The chapter closes with a wish that the LORD bless the reader out of Zion, that he see the good of Jerusalem all his life and see his children's children, and with a declaration of peace upon Israel.

The LORD is the one who bestows blessing on those who fear him, and the text invokes him to bless the reader out of Zion. He is the source of the prosperity, family and well-being described, and the unit ends with a prayer for peace upon Israel.

l: everyone who fears the LORD, Psalms, Chapter 128
s: Everyone who fears the LORD and walks in his ways is called blessed. Such a person will eat the labor of his hands, be happy and fare well, with a wife like a fruitful vine and children like olive shoots around his table. The text states that this is how the man who fears the LORD is blessed.

Blessing is pronounced on everyone who fears the LORD and is described as enjoying the fruit of one's labor, happiness, well-being, and a flourishing household. It is also expressed as a wish: that the LORD bless the reader out of Zion, that he see the good of Jerusalem all his days, and that he see his children's children.

Chapter 129 is a Song of Ascents in which Israel is called to declare that it has been afflicted many times from its youth but never overcome. The affliction is pictured as plowers making long furrows on Israel's back. The LORD is described as righteous and as having cut apart the cords of the wicked. The psalm then asks that all who hate Zion be disappointed and turned backward, becoming like grass on the housetops that withers before it grows. It ends by saying that no reaper or binder of sheaves is filled by such grass, and that passersby do not offer the blessing of the LORD's name to them.
Israel is called to say that it has been afflicted many times from its youth up, yet has not been prevailed against. Its back is pictured as plowed, with long furrows made by the plowers.
The LORD is declared righteous. He has cut apart the cords of the wicked.
Zion is named as the object of hatred by those who are wished to be disappointed and turned backward. No action by Zion itself is described in this unit.

l: afflicters (those who afflicted Israel), Psalms, Chapter 129
s: They have afflicted Israel many times from its youth up, plowing its back with long furrows. They have not prevailed against Israel.
The LORD has cut apart the cords of the wicked. They are pictured as being restrained or freed from their hold by this act.

The psalm asks that they be disappointed and turned backward, and be like grass on the housetops that withers before it grows up. Reapers and sheaf-binders gain nothing from them, and passersby do not bless them in the LORD's name.

Chapter 130, a Song of Ascents, is a prayer in which the psalmist cries to the LORD out of the depths and asks the Lord to hear the voice of his petitions. The psalmist observes that no one could stand if the LORD kept a record of sins, but that forgiveness is with the LORD, and therefore he is feared. The psalmist declares that his soul waits and hopes in the LORD's word, longing for the Lord more than watchmen long for the morning. The psalmist then urges Israel to hope in the LORD, because loving kindness and abundant redemption are with him. The chapter ends with the promise that the LORD will redeem Israel from all their sins.

The LORD is the one to whom the psalmist cries out of the depths and whom he asks to hear his petitions. He is described as having forgiveness, loving kindness and abundant redemption, and is feared because of his forgiveness. He is said to be the one who will redeem Israel from all their sins.
Israel is urged by the psalmist to hope in the LORD because of his loving kindness and abundant redemption. The chapter closes with the statement that the LORD will redeem Israel from all their sins.

The psalmist cries to the LORD out of the depths and pleads for the Lord to hear his petitions. He waits and hopes in the LORD's word, his soul longing for the Lord more than watchmen long for the morning, and he then exhorts Israel to hope in the LORD.
The psalmist says that if the LORD kept a record of sins, no one could stand. The chapter ends with the promise that the LORD will redeem Israel from all their sins.
Forgiveness is said to be with the LORD, and the psalmist states that this is why he is feared. It answers the problem raised by the possibility of the LORD keeping a record of sins.
Abundant redemption is said to be with the LORD, as a reason for Israel to hope in him. The chapter concludes that he will redeem Israel from all their sins.

Chapter 131 is a short Song of Ascents attributed to David. The speaker addresses the LORD, declaring that his heart is not arrogant, his eyes are not lofty, and he does not concern himself with great matters or things too wonderful for him. He says he has stilled and quieted his soul, comparing it to a weaned child with its mother. The psalm closes with a call to Israel to hope in the LORD from now and forever.
The LORD is addressed directly by the speaker, who affirms before him a humble heart and non-arrogant eyes. At the close, Israel is urged to hope in the LORD from this time forward and forever more.
Israel is addressed in the final verse and told to hope in the LORD from this time forward and forever more. This is the only instruction the psalm gives to others.

l: speaker (author of the psalm), Psalms, Chapter 131
s: The speaker, identified in the heading as David, tells the LORD that his heart is not arrogant, his eyes are not lofty, and he does not concern himself with great matters or things too wonderful for him. He says he has stilled and quieted his soul, likening it to a weaned child with its mother. He then calls on Israel to hope in the LORD.

l: weaned child (the speaker's simile), Psalms, Chapter 131
s: The weaned child, shown with its mother, is the image the speaker uses for his stilled and quieted soul. The comparison is stated twice in verse 2: his soul is like a weaned child within him.

Chapter 132, a Song of Ascents, asks the LORD to remember David and his affliction, recalling David's oath not to rest until he found a place for the LORD, a dwelling for the Mighty One of Jacob. The people report hearing of it in Ephrathah, finding it in the field of Jaar, and resolve to worship at his footstool, then call on the LORD to arise into his resting place with the ark of his strength. They plead for the sake of David, and recall the LORD's sworn promise that David's descendants will sit on his throne forever if they keep the covenant and testimony. The LORD is said to have chosen Zion as his habitation and resting place forever, where he promises to bless her provision, satisfy her poor with bread, clothe her priests with salvation, make David's horn bud, and shame his enemies while David's crown shines.

The LORD is asked to remember David and to arise into his resting place with the ark of his strength. He is said to have sworn to David in truth to set David's offspring on his throne, and to have chosen Zion as his habitation. He promises to bless Zion's provision, satisfy her poor with bread, clothe her priests with salvation, make David's horn bud, ordain a lamp for his anointed, and clothe the anointed's enemies with shame.

David is remembered for all his affliction and for the oath he swore to the LORD not to enter his house, go to bed, or sleep until he found a place for the LORD. The LORD swore to him that the fruit of his body would sit on his throne. The LORD will make his horn bud, ordain a lamp for his anointed, and make the crown of his anointed shine.

Zion is described as chosen by the LORD and desired for his habitation. The LORD declares it his resting place forever and promises to bless her provision, satisfy her poor with bread, and clothe her priests with salvation so that her saints shout aloud for joy.

The LORD promises to set the fruit of David's body on his throne. If David's children keep the LORD's covenant and the testimony he will teach them, their children will also sit on the throne forevermore.

David swore and vowed to the Mighty One of Jacob that he would not enter his house, go up into his bed, or give sleep to his eyes or slumber to his eyelids. He would not rest until he found a place for the LORD, a dwelling for the Mighty One of Jacob.

l: covenant (the LORD's covenant with David), Psalms, Chapter 132
s: The LORD has sworn in truth to David and will not turn from it, promising to set David's offspring on his throne. The promise extends to later generations on the condition that David's children keep the covenant and the testimony the LORD will teach them.

l: dwelling place (the LORD's dwelling), Psalms, Chapter 132
s: David vowed to find a place for the LORD, a dwelling for the Mighty One of Jacob. The people heard of it in Ephrathah, found it in the field of Jaar, and resolve to go into his dwelling place and worship at his footstool. The LORD later declares Zion his resting place forever, where he will live because he desired it.

Chapter 133 is a short Song of Ascents attributed to David. It praises the goodness and pleasantness of brothers living together in unity. It compares this unity to precious oil running down Aaron's head, beard, and the edge of his robes, and to the dew of Hermon falling on the hills of Zion. It closes by saying that in that place the LORD gives the blessing, life forevermore.
Brothers are described as living together in unity, which the speaker calls good and pleasant. Their shared life is the subject the whole chapter praises.
Unity among brothers is declared both good and pleasant. It is illustrated by two images, the precious oil on Aaron's head and the dew of Hermon on Zion's hills.

l: precious oil (on Aaron's head), Psalms, Chapter 133
s: The precious oil is poured on the head and runs down onto the beard, Aaron's beard, and then to the edge of his robes. It serves as the first comparison for the goodness of unity.
The dew of Hermon is said to come down on the hills of Zion. It serves as the second comparison for the pleasantness of brothers' unity.
The LORD is said to give the blessing, life forevermore, in the place where the dew of Hermon falls on the hills of Zion.
The blessing is given by the LORD there on the hills of Zion. It is identified as life forevermore.

Chapter 134 is a short song of ascents that calls on the servants of the LORD to praise him. The servants are described as standing by night in the LORD's house. They are told to lift up their hands in the sanctuary and praise the LORD. The chapter ends with a blessing: may the LORD, who made heaven and earth, bless the listener from Zion.

The LORD is the one the servants are urged to praise, both at his house and in the sanctuary. He is described as the maker of heaven and earth, and the closing verse asks that he bless the listener from Zion.

l: servants of the LORD, Psalms, Chapter 134
s: The servants of the LORD are addressed directly and called to praise him. They are described as standing by night in the LORD's house, and are told to lift up their hands in the sanctuary and praise the LORD.
The LORD's house is the place where the servants of the LORD stand by night. It is also referred to as the sanctuary, where hands are to be lifted in praise.

Chapter 135 is a call to praise the LORD, addressed to his servants who stand in his house and to the houses of Israel, Aaron, and Levi and those who fear him. It says the LORD chose Jacob and Israel as his own possession, is great and above all gods, and does whatever he pleases in heaven, earth, and the seas, including producing clouds, lightning, rain, and wind. It recalls how he struck the firstborn of Egypt and sent signs and wonders against Pharaoh and his servants, then struck many nations and killed kings such as Sihon of the Amorites and Og of Bashan, giving their land to Israel as a heritage. It contrasts the LORD, whose name endures forever, with the idols of the nations, which are silver and gold made by human hands and cannot speak, see, hear, or breathe, and says those who make and trust them will be like them. It ends with a blessing on the LORD from Zion, where he dwells in Jerusalem.

The LORD is called to be praised as good, great, and above all gods, and is said to do whatever he pleases in heaven, earth, and the seas. He causes clouds, lightning, rain, and wind, struck Egypt's firstborn, killed mighty kings including Sihon and Og, and gave their land to Israel. His name and renown endure through all generations, he will judge his people and have compassion on his servants, and he dwells in Jerusalem.

Israel is said to be chosen by the LORD as his own possession, along with Jacob. The LORD gave Israel the lands of Sihon, Og, and the kingdoms of Canaan as a heritage. The houses of Israel, Aaron, and Levi are each called to praise the LORD.
Egypt is the place where the LORD struck the firstborn of both man and animal. He sent signs and wonders into its midst, against Pharaoh and all his servants.

l: those who fear the LORD, Psalms, Chapter 135
s: The servants of the LORD, who stand in the LORD's house and in the courts of God's house, are called to praise the LORD and his name. The LORD is said to have compassion on his servants when he judges his people.

l: idol makers and trusters, Psalms, Chapter 135
s: The idols of the nations are described as silver and gold, the work of men's hands. They have mouths, eyes, and ears but cannot speak, see, or hear, and have no breath. Those who make them and trust in them will be like them.

Chapter 136 is a call to give thanks to the LORD, the God of gods, Lord of lords and God of heaven, with each verse closing on the refrain that his loving kindness endures forever. It praises him as creator who made the heavens, spread the earth above the waters, and made the sun, moon and stars. It recounts how he struck down the Egyptian firstborn, brought Israel out with a strong hand and outstretched arm, divided the Red Sea, and overthrew Pharaoh and his army. It then recalls how he led his people through the wilderness, struck down Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan, and gave their land as a heritage to Israel his servant. It ends by noting that he remembered his people in their low estate, delivered them from adversaries, and gives food to every creature.

The LORD is called good and is praised as God of gods, Lord of lords and God of heaven, who alone does great wonders. He is credited with making the heavens, earth and lights, striking the Egyptian firstborn, delivering Israel, defeating kings, and giving food to every creature.

Israel is brought out from among the Egyptians with a strong hand and outstretched arm, and made to pass through the middle of the Red Sea. Led through the wilderness, Israel receives the land of Sihon and Og as an inheritance and is called God's servant.
The Red Sea is divided apart by God so that Israel can pass through its middle. Pharaoh and his army are overthrown in it.

God's loving kindness is declared to endure forever in the refrain that ends every one of the chapter's 26 verses. It is tied to his acts as creator, deliverer, giver of land, rememberer of the lowly and provider of food.

The Exodus is told through God striking the Egyptian firstborn and bringing Israel out with a strong hand and outstretched arm. It continues with the division of the Red Sea, Israel's passage, the overthrow of Pharaoh's army, and the leading of the people through the wilderness.

The exiles sit by the rivers of Babylon and weep as they remember Zion, hanging their harps on the willows. Their captors and tormentors demand songs of joy, and the exiles ask how they can sing the LORD's song in a foreign land. The speaker swears an oath that his right hand and tongue should fail him if he forgets Jerusalem or does not prefer it above his chief joy. He asks the LORD to remember the children of Edom, who urged that Jerusalem be razed to its foundation. He closes by pronouncing happy whoever repays the doomed Daughter of Babylon, including the one who dashes her little ones against the rock.
Babylon is the foreign land where the exiles sit weeping by its rivers. The willows there hold the harps the exiles have hung up.
Zion is what the exiles remember as they weep by the rivers of Babylon. The captors ask for 'songs of Zion', which marks it as the source of the songs the exiles once sang.

Jerusalem is the city the speaker vows never to forget, saying his right hand and tongue should fail him if he does. He prefers it above his chief joy. The children of Edom are said to have called for it to be razed to its foundation.
The LORD is the one whose song the exiles cannot sing in a foreign land. The speaker calls on him to remember the children of Edom for what they said on the day of Jerusalem.
The children of Edom are accused of saying 'Raze it! Raze it even to its foundation!' on the day of Jerusalem. The speaker asks the LORD to remember this against them.

The Daughter of Babylon is addressed as doomed to destruction. The speaker declares happy whoever repays her as she has done to the exiles, and whoever takes and dashes her little ones against the rock.
The captives sit by the rivers of Babylon and weep as they remember Zion. They hang up their harps on the willows and ask how they can sing the LORD's song in a foreign land.

l: captors (those who led us captive), Psalms, Chapter 137
s: The captors, who also tormented the exiles, ask for songs and demand songs of joy, saying 'Sing us one of the songs of Zion!'
The songs of Zion are what the captors demand the exiles sing for their amusement. The exiles hang up their harps and ask how they can sing the LORD's song in a foreign land.

The speaker speaks first as part of the exiles ('we'), then in the first person as 'I'. He vows loyalty to Jerusalem with a self-curse and calls on the LORD to remember Edom. He pronounces happy whoever repays the Daughter of Babylon.

Chapter 138, attributed to David, is a psalm of thanksgiving addressed to the LORD. David pledges to give thanks with his whole heart, sing praises before the gods, and bow toward the holy temple because of the LORD's loving kindness, truth, and exalted Name and Word. He recalls that the LORD answered him on the day he called and strengthened his soul. He says all the kings of the earth will thank the LORD and sing of his ways after hearing his words. David affirms that the LORD looks after the lowly, knows the proud from afar, will revive him in trouble and save him from his enemies, and he asks the LORD not to forsake the works of his hands.

The LORD is thanked and praised for his loving kindness and truth, and his Name and Word are said to be exalted above all. He answered David on the day he called, strengthened his soul, looks after the lowly while knowing the proud from afar, and is trusted to revive David, stretch out his hand against enemies, and save him with his right hand. His loving kindness is said to endure forever, and he is asked not to forsake the works of his own hands.

David, named as the author, vows to thank the LORD with his whole heart, sing praises before the gods, and bow toward the holy temple. He recounts that the LORD answered him and strengthened his soul. He expresses confidence that the LORD will revive him in trouble and save him from the wrath of his enemies, and he asks that the LORD not forsake the works of his hands.
